summary: US-dollar venture funds in China are pulling back as Beijing's tech crackdown, tighter overseas IPO rules and US investment restrictions shrink opportunities. Some fund managers are following Chinese-founded startups ("guihai") that expand abroad, visiting the Bay Area to source deals, but face trust and geopolitical hurdles. PitchBook data shows a sharp fall in US-backed deals, with no recovery expected soon.
one_line: US-dollar VC funds in China are shrinking amid regulatory and geopolitical pressure and increasingly chase Chinese-founded startups expanding overseas.
key_facts: In August 2023, President Joe Biden signed an executive order barring US investments in three strategically critical Chinese sectors: artificial intelligence, quantum computing and semiconductors.
In 2022, US-headquartered VCs invested just $14.5 billion in Chinese companies, compared to $45.4 billion the year before, per PitchBook.
The number of deals with US investors nearly halved to 595 in 2022, and the share of deals with US investor participation fell to 18.2% after hovering above 30% for half a decade.
HongShan (formerly Sequoia Capital China) completed just 47 deals in the first three quarters of 2023, versus 99 in the same period of 2022, according to Crunchbase.
Despite splitting off its China operation, Sequoia still faces scrutiny from the US government over its decades of activity in China.
VCs fear their portfolio companies could face the fate of Ant Group, whose IPO was called off, and Didi, which was delisted from New York after a data security probe.
Zhipu AI, a Chinese challenger to OpenAI, raised financing in RMB instead of USD, reflecting the growing role of domestic RMB funds in critical tech.
Chinese entrepreneurs who return overseas are called guihai ("return overseas"), a reversal of haigui ("sea turtles" who returned to China).
Launching an AI service in China requires navigating licensing for large language models, regulatory approval of algorithms and costly censorship mechanisms.
A San Francisco-based Chinese founder said to raise local money you need to speak like a local, have taken no Chinese VC money, have all staff in the US and be pursuing a green card.
PitchBook predicts VC activity with US participation in China will hit a nine-year low in 2023 and a decade low in 2024.
Many Chinese general partners are sourcing capital from the Middle East, and Japan is a popular market for Chinese SaaS startups going abroad.
The article is based on interviews with five China-based VCs and six diaspora Chinese entrepreneurs, all anonymous.
